qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with rabies following a stray dog bite. The neurological symptoms progress rapidly. What is the fundamental mechanism by which the rabies virus travels from the peripheral bite site to the central nervous system?
o: Virus moves trans‑synaptically across capillary endothelial gaps in local muscle tissue.
Virus spreads hematogenously inside infected monocytes that cross the blood‑brain barrier.
Virus drains via lymphatics to regional nodes, then to the thoracic duct and jugular vein.
Virus diffuses passively through interstitial fascial planes around skeletal muscle fibers.
Virus travels retrogradely along peripheral sensory and motor axons toward the central nervous system.
qs.e: Rabies virus travels from the inoculation site to the central nervous system exclusively via retrograde axonal transport.

qs.q: A patient's lab results show low arterial carbon dioxide tension resulting from hyperventilation. How does the central nervous system respond to this state?
o: Reduction of ventilatory drive via receptors
Stimulation of medullary inspiratory neurons
Secretion of bicarbonate by choroid plexus
Constriction of cerebral blood vessels
Activation of peripheral oxygen sensors
qs.e: Low PCO2 reduces brain extracellular hydrogen ion concentration, decreasing central chemoreceptor stimulation and suppressing ventilation.

qs.q: During a physiological evaluation of respiratory control, arterial PCO2 rises. Which central nervous system structure serves as the primary sensor detecting this change via alterations in cerebrospinal fluid pH?

Aortic bodies located along the aortic arch wall
Dorsal respiratory group driving phrenic nerve activation
Solitary tract nucleus integrating sensory visceral input
Central chemoreceptors located on the ventral medulla
qs.e: Central chemoreceptors on the ventral medullary surface sense changes in CSF pH resulting from carbon dioxide diffusion across the blood-brain barrier.

Preference for anaerobic environments in ventricles
Rapid replication within resident microglial cells
Destruction of the blood‑brain barrier via toxins
Enhanced affinity for myelin basic protein targets

CD4 molecules present on the surface of local dendritic and Langerhans cells.
Sialoglycoproteins expressed abundantly on epithelial cells of the upper airway.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors located at the neuromuscular junction synapses.

Retrograde axonal transport utilizing fast motor protein machinery

qs.q: A patient with an inherited urea cycle defect presents with hyperammonemia and neurological impairment. Which specific metabolic intermediate is most directly depleted in the central nervous system due to ammonia detoxification?
o: Oxaloacetate consumption via cellular transamination pathways
Malate accumulation inhibiting cytosolic malate dehydrogenase
Pyruvate diversion into peripheral tissue lactate production
Alpha-ketoglutarate depletion from the tricarboxylic acid cycle

ai.title: Central Nervous System in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, the control centre for all body functions. In low‑resource settings, infections, malnutrition and trauma are the main threats. Rapid bedside assessment and targeted investigations guide life‑saving treatment.

sections.p: The CNS comprises the brain, spinal cord and meninges. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and examination, then uses simple imaging or CSF studies when available.
b: History of fever, seizures, altered consciousness
Neuro‑deficits, papilledema, neck stiffness

t.b: Rule out meningitis or TB meningitis – CSF opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, Xpert MTB/RIF

sections.p: Severity is graded by level of consciousness and focal deficits. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the most useful tool in children.
b: GCS 13‑15: mild
GCS 9‑12: moderate
GCS 3‑8: severe

sections.p: In East Africa, infections dominate. Malnutrition, HIV, malaria and trauma also contribute.
b: Bacterial meningitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae)
Tuberculous meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV)
Malaria‑associated cerebral malaria
Traumatic brain injury
Sickle‑cell crises

sections.p: Presentation varies with age and cause. Common features include fever, seizures, vomiting, lethargy and focal neuro‑signs.
b: Seizure type: generalized tonic‑clonic, focal, febrile
Headache, neck stiffness, photophobia
Altered sensorium, vomiting, papilledema

sections.p: Use the simplest tests that answer a specific clinical question. When a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and supportive care.

t.b: High WBC suggests bacterial infection; low Hb may indicate anaemia complicating CNS disease
Positive test warrants immediate artesunate
Positive result starts anti‑TB therapy
Normal CT allows safe LP; abnormal CT requires neurosurgical input

sections.p: Certain signs predict poor outcome or need urgent intervention.
b: Severe headache with papilledema – raised intracranial pressure
Seizure >5 minutes – status epilepticus
Focal deficits – possible stroke or abscess
Unexplained bleeding – consider haemorrhagic stroke

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support vital functions and monitor for complications. Drug choice favours safety and availability.
b: Empiric antibiotics for bacterial meningitis: ceftriaxone + ampicillin (or cefotaxime + ampicillin)
Anti‑TB therapy: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol
Antifungals for cryptococcal meningitis: amphotericin B + flucytosine (if available)
Antimalarials: artesunate for cerebral malaria
Supportive care: maintain airway, oxygen, fluids, glucose, seizure control with phenobarbitone or phenytoin

sections.p: Early discharge planning, vaccination and community education reduce recurrence.
b: Ensure completion of full anti‑TB course
Vaccinate against Hib and pneumococcus
Educate caregivers on early signs of meningitis
Screen for HIV and provide ART

sections.p: Several conditions mimic CNS disease; recognising differences is key.
b: Febrile seizures – isolated seizure, no focal deficits
Sepsis with encephalopathy – diffuse, no focal signs
Traumatic brain injury – history of injury, focal deficits

sections.p: Some investigations may give false negatives or positives in low‑resource settings.
b: CSF glucose can be normal in TB meningitis if glucose is low systemically
Xpert MTB/RIF may miss paucibacillary TB
Rapid malaria tests may miss low parasitaemia

faq.q: Why is a lumbar puncture contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure?
faq.a: It can cause brain herniation by suddenly lowering CSF pressure.

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in suspected bacterial meningitis?
faq.a: Empiric ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) plus ampicillin to cover common organisms.

faq.q: How do you differentiate tuberculous meningitis from bacterial meningitis clinically?
faq.a: TB meningitis is slower, with chronic fever, cranial nerve palsies and a lymphocytic CSF; bacterial meningitis is acute with neutrophilic CSF and high opening pressure.

exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with fever, vomiting and a stiff neck. What is the first investigation you would do and why? — LP after normal CT to rule out meningitis, but only if no signs of raised ICP. A child with altered consciousness and a positive malaria rapid test. What is the next step? — Immediate artesunate and supportive care; do not delay for imaging. A 3‑year‑old with seizures and a history of sickle cell disease. What is the most likely cause and first treatment? — Acu

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused paediatric CNS history and systematic exam can often differentiate infection, metabolic disturbance, trauma or vascular cause even when investigations are limited.
b: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; days for meningitis, weeks for TBM, hours for trauma.
Fever pattern: continuous high fever suggests bacterial meningitis; intermittent spikes may occur in malaria.
Seizure description: generalized tonic‑clonic, focal, febrile, duration >5 min (status).
Associated symptoms: vomiting, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, rash, recent travel, sick contacts, HIV status, malnutrition.
Past medical history: sickle‑cell disease, HIV, previous CNS infection, trauma, drug/herbal exposure.
Vaccination record: pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, measles.

t.b: Ask: What is the child's alertness? Use GCS (eye, verbal, motor) for all ages; in infants use modified GCS. GCS 13‑15 = mild, 9‑12 = moderate, 3‑8 = severe. Does not quantify focal deficits.

Ask: Does passive knee extension cause pain? Positive Kernig = resistance to knee extension >30°. Brudzinski = involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion. Positive suggests meningeal irritation but can be absent in infants.
Ask: Is there optic disc swelling? Presence indicates raised intracranial pressure; absent does not rule it out, especially early or in optic nerve disease.

Ask: Any weakness, cranial nerve palsy, sensory loss? Test motor strength, cranial nerves, gait. Positive findings point to stroke, abscess, or severe encephalitis; bedside cannot locate lesion precisely.
Ask: Is there bulging fontanelle or irritability on handling? Bulging fontanelle suggests raised ICP; irritability is non‑specific. These signs cannot differentiate bacterial vs. viral meningitis.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use the simplest test that answers the clinical question; when a test is unavailable, rely on clinical probability and treat empirically.
b: Lumbar puncture – answers: type of meningitis, TBM, cryptococcal infection, cell count, protein, glucose, CrAg, PCR.
Rapid malaria test – answers: presence of Plasmodium falciparum; positive in cerebral malaria with coma.
Blood glucose – answers: hypoglycaemia as cause of altered sensorium; <2.2 mmol/L is critical.
Serum electrolytes – answers: hyponatraemia or hypernatraemia contributing to seizures.

t.b: Question: Is there pleocytosis? >5 cells/mm³ abnormal in children >1 yr; up to 30 cells/mm³ may be normal in neonates; up to 10 cells/mm³ in infants 1‑12 mo.
Question: Is protein elevated? >0.5 g/L suggests TBM or cryptococcal meningitis; lower values more typical of viral meningitis.
Question: Is glucose low? <2.2 mmol/L or CSF:serum ratio <0.5 supports bacterial or tuberculous meningitis.
Question: Is cryptococcal infection present? Titre >1:4 is highly suggestive of cryptococcal meningitis.
Question: Does the child have unrousable coma in malaria? Score <2 defines unrousable coma; use when malaria is endemic.
Question: Is Plasmodium falciparum present? Positive test plus clinical coma indicates cerebral malaria; negative test does not exclude malaria if microscopy unavailable.
Question: Is tissue hypoxia present? Lactate >2 mmol/L suggests severe sepsis or malaria; guide aggressive fluid resuscitation.
Question: Is there space‑occupying lesion, hydrocephalus, or infarct? Imaging confirms abscess, stroke, or raised ICP; unavailable → treat based on clinical picture.

sections.p: Classification integrates clinical state, CSF findings and aetiology to guide urgency of treatment.
b: Meningitis – bacterial if CSF: >1000 cells/mm³ neutrophils, protein >1 g/L, glucose <2.2 mmol/L; tuberculous if lymphocytic >10‑100 cells/mm³, protein >0.5 g/L, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, chronic course.
Cryptococcal meningitis – CSF CrAg >1:4, India‑ink positive, protein often >0.5 g/L, glucose low or normal.
Cerebral malaria – unrousable coma (Blantyre <2) + positive malaria test + no other cause.
Traumatic brain injury – history of head trauma, GCS <13, focal deficits, CT evidence of bleed or edema.
Status epilepticus – seizure >5 min or recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness; treat as emergency.

t.b: Mild 13‑15, moderate 9‑12, severe 3‑8; guides need for airway protection and intensive monitoring.
Papilledema, Cushing triad, decreasing GCS; indicates need for osmotherapy or neurosurgical referral.

sections.p: Several non‑infectious or alternative infections mimic CNS infection in low‑resource settings; careful history and targeted tests separate them.
b: Viral encephalitis (e.g., HSV) – fever, seizures, focal deficits; CSF lymphocytes, normal glucose, modest protein; PCR if available.
Acute bacterial sinusitis with orbital cellulitis – facial pain, periorbital swelling; no meningeal signs; CT sinus helpful.
Septicemia with metabolic encephalopathy – low glucose, high lactate, no CSF pleocytosis; treat underlying sepsis.
Neuro‑leptospirosis – exposure to contaminated water, conjunctival suffusion; CSF may show mild pleocytosis, normal glucose; serology required.

t.b: Points: focal temporal lobe signs, behavioural change. Separate by CSF PCR or empiric acyclovir if PCR unavailable.
Points: hypoglycaemia, hepatic/renal failure, urea cycle disorder. CSF normal; treat underlying metabolic derangement.
Points: subacute fever, focal deficit, ring‑enhancing lesion on imaging. CSF may be normal; need imaging or surgical drainage.
Points: exposure history, conjunctival suffusion, aseptic meningitis picture. Serology or MAT confirms; treat with doxycycline.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides acute CNS emergencies in low‑resource paediatric settings, moving from stabilisation to definitive therapy and clear triggers for escalation or referral.
b: 1. Airway, breathing, circulation – protect airway, give high‑flow oxygen, treat hypoglycaemia immediately.
2. Rapid bedside assessment – GCS, focal deficits, papilledema, seizures; start empiric antimicrobial within 1 hour if infection suspected.

3. Targeted therapy – give appropriate antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone for bacterial meningitis), antitubercular drugs for TBM, amphotericin B plus flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis, artesunate for cerebral malaria.
4. Adjuncts – dexamethasone for bacterial meningitis in children >6 weeks, mannitol or hypertonic saline for raised ICP, antiepileptics for seizures, fluid‑electrolyte balance.
5. Monitoring – hourly GCS, pupil size, seizure activity, urine output, vital signs; repeat lumbar puncture if no clinical improvement.
6. Escalation – worsening GCS, new focal deficit, refractory seizures, ICP signs, or laboratory deterioration → transfer to higher‑level centre.
7. Referral – when neurosurgical intervention, intensive ventilation, or advanced imaging is required.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse reactions and interactions for the core drug groups used in paediatric CNS infections and emergencies.
b: Ceftriaxone – biliary sludge; monitor for abdominal pain, switch to cefotaxime if problematic.
Dexamethasone – hyperglycaemia, GI bleeding; give proton‑pump inhibitor in at‑risk children.
Artesunate – delayed haemolysis; check haemoglobin at day 7 and day 14 post‑treatment.
Amphotericin B – nephrotoxicity, electrolyte loss; hydrate aggressively, replace potassium and magnesium.
Flucytosine – bone‑marrow suppression; obtain baseline CBC and repeat twice weekly.
Phenobarbital – respiratory depression; avoid in severe coma, monitor respiratory rate.
Mannitol – renal failure risk; stop if urine output falls below 0.5 mL/kg/h.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae that demand urgent higher‑level care.
b: Status epilepticus lasting >5 minutes – give benzodiazepine, load second‑line antiepileptic, call for intensive care.
Rising intracranial pressure – papilledema, Cushing’s triad, deteriorating GCS – start osmotherapy, consider ventriculostomy, refer.
Hydrocephalus on repeat imaging – neurosurgical drainage required.
Severe anaemia or haemolysis after artesunate – transfuse, monitor renal function.
Renal failure from amphotericin B – discontinue, switch to fluconazole if possible, arrange dialysis.

sections.p: Conditions that modify presentation, laboratory interpretation and therapeutic choices in paediatric CNS disease.
b: HIV – lower CSF white‑cell count, higher protein, increased risk of cryptococcal and TB meningitis; use cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, avoid steroids unless TBM.
Malnutrition – blunted fever, altered CSF glucose thresholds; give higher caloric support, monitor electrolytes closely.
Pregnancy (adolescent mothers) – avoid tetracyclines, use ceftriaxone and ampicillin; consider fetal effects of dexamethasone.
Diabetes mellitus – hyperglycaemia worsened by steroids; check glucose hourly, adjust insulin.
Herbal remedies (e.g., traditional plant extracts) – possible hepatotoxicity, interfere with drug metabolism; obtain full medication history.
Alcohol use (older adolescents) – potentiates CNS depressant effects of phenobarbital; limit sedatives.
Renal failure – dose‑adjust ceftriaxone, avoid amphotericin B if GFR < 30 mL/min; use fluconazole instead.
Liver failure – avoid high‑dose paracetamol, monitor bilirubin with antitubercular drugs.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant patients, the elderly and HIV‑positive individuals in low‑resource environments.
b: Children – use weight‑based drug classes (e.g., ceftriaxone, artesunate); assess developmental milestones for neurological sequelae.
Pregnancy – prioritize drugs with Category B safety (ceftriaxone, ampicillin); avoid aminoglycosides when possible; monitor fetal heart rate.
Elderly – higher risk of drug‑induced delirium; start low‑dose antiepileptics, watch for renal clearance decline.
People with HIV – start antiretroviral therapy after acute infection stabilises; screen for opportunistic CNS pathogens, give prophylactic cotrimoxazole.

Low‑resource settings – if lumbar puncture unavailable, use clinical algorithm (fever + neck stiffness + altered consciousness) to start empiric therapy; use rapid antigen tests for cryptococcus; rely on clinical signs for raised ICP.

facts: CSF white cell count >5/mm³ abnormal in children >1 yr; neonates ≤30/mm³ and infants 1‑12 mo ≤10/mm³ may be normal.
Blantyre Coma Scale <2 defines unrousable coma in cerebral malaria.
CSF protein >0.5 g/L suggests TB or cryptococcal meningitis.
CSF glucose <2.2 mmol/L or CSF:serum ratio <0.5 indicates bacterial or tuberculous meningitis.
Cryptococcal antigen titre >1:4 in CSF is diagnostic of cryptococcal meningitis.
GCS 13‑15 mild, 9‑12 moderate, 3‑8 severe for all ages.
Status epilepticus defined as seizure >5 min or two seizures without full recovery.
Papilledema indicates raised intracranial pressure; urgent neuro‑imaging required.

vivas.q: What is the first bedside investigation for a child with fever, vomiting and neck stiffness?
vivas.a: Perform a lumbar puncture after stabilising airway, breathing, circulation and ensuring no signs of raised intracranial pressure.

vivas.q: How does the CNS respond to low arterial CO₂ from hyperventilation?
vivas.a: Central chemoreceptors decrease ventilation, leading to a rise in PaCO₂ to restore pH.

vivas.q: Which CNS structure senses rising arterial PCO₂ via CSF pH changes?
vivas.a: The ventral respiratory group in the medulla oblongata, especially the retrotrapezoid nucleus.

vivas.q: What receptor does rabies virus glycoprotein bind to for neuronal entry?
vivas.a: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, also neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM).

vivas.q: Explain the mechanism by which rabies reaches the CNS after a peripheral bite.
vivas.a: The virus travels retrograde along peripheral nerves via dynein‑mediated axonal transport to the spinal cord and brain.

vivas.q: Why does Cryptococcus neoformans preferentially infect the CNS?
vivas.a: Its capsule resists phagocytosis and it crosses the blood‑brain barrier using a ‘Trojan‑horse’ mechanism within macrophages.

vivas.q: Which metabolic intermediate is depleted in the brain of a hyperammonaemic urea‑cycle patient?
vivas.a: α‑ketoglutarate, as ammonia is detoxified to glutamine consuming it.

vivas.q: Name the resident mononuclear phagocytes of the CNS that respond to injury.
When should you avoid lumbar puncture in a child with suspected meningitis?
vivas.a: If there are signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilledema, focal neurological deficit, or a GCS ≤8.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate bacterial from tuberculous meningitis on CSF analysis?
vivas.a: Bacterial meningitis: WBC >1000/mm³, neutrophil predominance, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, protein >1 g/L. TBM: moderate pleocytosis (100‑500), lymphocyte predominance, glucose low‑normal, protein 0.5‑1 g/L.

vivas.q: What is the immediate management of status epilepticus in a child?
vivas.a: Secure airway, give benzodiazepine (e.g., IV diazepam), then load a longer‑acting antiepileptic (e.g., phenobarbital).

vivas.q: Which bedside sign helps detect raised intracranial pressure in a comatose child?
vivas.a: Papilledema on fundoscopic exam; a swollen optic disc with blurred margins indicates increased ICP.

vivas.q: What is the role of the Blantyre Coma Scale in cerebral malaria?
vivas.a: It grades consciousness; a score <2 defines unrousable coma and mandates urgent antimalarial therapy and supportive care.

vivas.q: Why is dexamethasone avoided in cryptococcal meningitis?
vivas.a: It impairs fungal clearance and worsens outcomes; antifungal therapy alone is recommended.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify the presentation of meningitis in children?
vivas.a: Opportunistic pathogens (Cryptococcus, CMV) are more common; CSF may show lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose despite normal WBC count.

vivas.q: What is the next step after a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen test?
vivas.a: Start induction therapy with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, followed by fluconazole consolidation.

vivas.q: When is a CT scan preferred before lumbar puncture?
vivas.a: When there are focal deficits, papilledema, seizures, or a GCS ≤8 suggesting possible mass effect.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions for a child with possible CNS infection?
vivas.a: Onset and pattern of fever, recent travel, immunisation status, exposure to sick contacts, HIV status, malaria exposure, trauma, sickle‑cell disease, and seizure history.

mcqs.q: A 4‑year‑old from a malaria‑endemic area presents with fever, seizures and a Blantyre Coma Scale of 1. Which finding best confirms cerebral malaria?
o: Peripheral smear showing asexual Plasmodium falciparum forms
Elevated CSF protein >1 g/L
Positive blood culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae
MRI showing diffuse edema
mcqs.e: Cerebral malaria diagnosis requires asexual parasites on peripheral smear plus unrousable coma.

mcqs.q: A child with suspected meningitis has CSF: WBC 8/mm³, protein 0.6 g/L, glucose 2.0 mmol/L (serum glucose 5.5 mmol/L). Which organism is most likely?
o: Neisseria meningitidis
Haemophilus influenzae
Cryptococcus neoformans
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
mcqs.e: TB meningitis often shows modest pleocytosis, protein >0.5 g/L and low glucose.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to immediate lumbar puncture?
o: Fever of 38.5 °C
Generalised tonic‑clonic seizure lasting 2 min
Mild neck stiffness
Papilledema on fundoscopy
mcqs.e: Papilledema indicates raised ICP; LP could cause herniation.

mcqs.q: Which CNS structure detects changes in CSF pH due to hypercapnia?
o: Area postrema
Retrotrapezoid nucleus
Nucleus tractus solitarius
Substantia nigra
mcqs.e: The retrotrapezoid nucleus contains central chemoreceptors sensitive to CSF pH.

mcqs.q: A 6‑year‑old with sickle‑cell disease presents with acute severe headache, vomiting and papilledema. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Ischaemic stroke
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Migraine
mcqs.e: Sickle‑cell disease predisposes to cerebral venous sinus thrombosis presenting with raised ICP.

mcqs.q: Which sign is NOT reliably assessed at the bedside for raised intracranial pressure?
o: Kernig's sign
Cushing's triad
Papilledema
Abnormal post‑uring pupil response
mcqs.e: Kernig's sign indicates meningeal irritation, not ICP.

cases.v: A 7‑year‑old boy from a rural Kenyan hospital presents with 2 days of fever, vomiting, and a stiff neck. He is alert, GCS 15, but has papilledema. No focal deficits.

qs.q: What is the immediate next step?
qs.a: Stabilise airway and give empiric ceftriaxone plus vancomycin after obtaining blood cultures; defer lumbar puncture until CT rules out mass effect.

qs.q: Which CSF findings would confirm bacterial meningitis?
qs.a: WBC >1000/mm³ neutrophil predominance, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, protein >1 g/L, positive Gram stain.

qs.q: If CSF culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae, what is the definitive therapy?
qs.a: Continue high‑dose ceftriaxone; add dexamethasone before or with first antibiotic dose to reduce neurologic complications.

cases.v: A 3‑year‑old girl with known HIV (CD4 12 %) presents with headache, photophobia, and low‑grade fever for 5 days. Fundoscopy shows papilledema. CSF opening pressure is 280 mmH₂O, protein 0.7 g/L, glucose 2.0 mmol/L, CrAg titre 1:8.

qs.a: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, followed by fluconazole consolidation.

qs.q: Why should steroids be avoided in this case?
qs.a: Steroids impair fungal clearance and increase mortality in cryptococcal meningitis.

mistakes: Using the adult CSF white‑cell cut‑off (>5/mm³) for neonates, leading to over‑diagnosis of meningitis.
Assuming a Blantyre Coma Scale of 3 indicates cerebral malaria; the correct cut‑off for unrousable coma is <2.
Interpreting CSF protein >1 g/L as specific for bacterial meningitis; TB and cryptococcal meningitis also raise protein above 0.5 g/L.
Starting dexamethasone in cryptococcal meningitis, which worsens outcomes.
Performing lumbar puncture without a CT scan when papilledema or focal deficits are present.
Neglecting to add pyridoxine to anti‑TB drugs in children, risking peripheral neuropathy.
Confusing hyperventilation‑induced hypocapnia response (decreased ventilation) with hypercapnia response (increased ventilation).
Failing to consider HIV‑related opportunistic pathogens, leading to missed diagnoses.

When should you avoid lumbar puncture in a child with suspected meningitis? — If there are signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilledema, focal neurological deficit, or a GCS ≤8.

How do you differentiate bacterial from tuberculous meningitis on CSF analysis? — Bacterial meningitis: WBC >1000/mm³, neutrophil predominance, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, protein >1 g/L. TBM: moderate pleocytosis (100‑500), lymphocyte predominance, glucose low‑normal, protein 0.5‑1 g/L.
What is the immediate management of status epilepticus in a child? — Secure airway, give benzodiazepine (e.g., IV diazepam), then load a longer‑acting antiepileptic (e.g., phenobarbital).
Which bedside sign helps detect raised intracranial pressure in a comatose child? — Papilledema on fundoscopic exam; a swollen optic disc with blurred margins indicates increased ICP.
What is the role of the Blantyre Coma Scale in cerebral malaria? — It grades consciousness; a score <2 defines unrousable coma and mandates urgent antimalarial therapy and supportive care.
Why is dexamethasone avoided in cryptococcal meningitis? — It impairs fungal clearance and worsens outcomes; antifungal therapy alone is recommended.
